text.p: The Australian cash grains market weakened further in the past week, leaving traders divided on whether the market is in for further falls or about to turn up.
Wheat, sorghum and other grain prices fell during the week, while wheat futures prices also edged back.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB), in its routine adjustment of pools prices in the week, left most prices steady while raising prices for premium quality Prime Hard and Australian Hard by A$5.00 a tonne each to reflect changing price differentials in international markets.
"There's still not that much excitement," said Peter Howard of New England Agricultural Traders. The group's Kansas City office was now looking for a slight move upward, he said.
Howard said he leant toward the bullish side, hoping the market had touched bottom.
Guy Allen of GrainCorp was less sure. "It'll probably continue to work a little lower," he said.
But U.S. corn was now set to lead both wheat and coarse grains.
"The next six weeks will tell on that, depending on frost, crop size, it's anybody's guess," he said.

One of the more interesting futures market views during the week was from Phil Lindsay of Ord Minnett Jardine Fleming Futures Ltd. Chartists saw January futures, now that it has broken through A$190, headed down to A$178 a tonne, he said.
On the week's cash market trading, "everything's reasonably weak," Howard said.
On his book, cash sorghum eased A$4-A$5 over the week in little activity.
Sydney sorghum sold at A$200 September delivery on Friday after trading at A$205 on Monday. November sorghum was bid at A$208 on Friday, down about A$7 on the week, he said.
Wheat cash prices weakened over the week, with feed wheat in Queensland's Darling Downs traded down to A$200 on Friday from A$215 on Monday. "Demand is reasonably weak," he said.
Old crop barley was hard to trade and activity slow, he said.
Allen saw the cash market working a little lower in the week, with prices down particularly on the last two days of the week.
Cash wheat to Newcastle traded as low as A$185, down A$2 to A$3, he said. Sorghum fell A$3 to A$5 a tonne to A$192 Newcastle bid or A$198 Sydney bid, he said.
Cash activity was fairly light in both new and old crop. "It's been fairly lacklustre," he said.
The AWB indicative price for new crop Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat fell by A$1 to A$181 over the week.
Australian wheat futures edged back during the week, with the most frequently-traded January contract falling to A$189.00 on Friday from A$190 the Friday before.
